cards.front: Where is stopping, standing or parking prohibited, including the hydrant distance?
cards.back: Except to avoid a conflict with other traffic or to obey a law, officer or signal, stopping, standing or parking is prohibited on a sidewalk, in front of a public or private driveway, within an intersection, within fifteen feet of a fire hydrant, and on a crosswalk.

cards.front: What distances from a crosswalk, stop sign and railroad rail forbid parking?
cards.back: Parking is also prohibited within twenty feet of a crosswalk at an intersection, within thirty feet of any stop sign or traffic control signal, in front of a wheelchair ramp or curb cut, and within fifty feet of the nearest rail of a railroad crossing.
cards.memory_hook: No parking: crosswalk, stop sign, rail

cards.front: Where else is parking prohibited, including bridges and mailboxes?
cards.back: Parking is further prohibited beside or opposite a street excavation or obstruction where it would obstruct traffic, on the traffic side of a vehicle stopped or parked at the curb, on any bridge, elevated structure or highway tunnel, and within twenty feet of a mailbox served by a carrier making daily deliveries by motor vehicle.

cards.front: Where is parking prohibited on highways, and what may a yellow curb mean?
cards.back: Parking is prohibited on any controlled-access highway, anywhere on a highway where it endangers the safety and convenience of the traveling public, and wherever official signs prohibit it, and a curb in a no-parking zone may be painted yellow.

cards.front: How do the no-parking distances climb from hydrant to railroad rail?
cards.back: The no-parking distances climb from fifteen feet at a fire hydrant, to twenty feet from a crosswalk at an intersection, to thirty feet from a stop sign or signal, to fifty feet from the nearest railroad rail.

cards.front: Which other spots are banned for parking, and what marks a no-parking zone?
cards.back: Within twenty feet of a daily-delivery mailbox, on any bridge or tunnel and on any controlled-access highway are all banned parking spots, and a yellow-painted curb marks a no-parking zone.

cards.front: Why must a driver learn correct turning procedures?
cards.back: Improper turns cause many traffic crashes and pedestrians and bicyclists are often their victims, so a driver must learn and follow correct turning procedures.

cards.front: What should you do before entering the turning lane?
cards.back: Prepare for a turn instead of deciding at the last moment, and before entering the turning lane signal, look in the mirrors and check the blind spot by glancing over the proper shoulder.

cards.front: How far ahead do you signal, and when do you slow?
cards.back: Signal at least one hundred feet before turning, slow down before the turn, and do not brake while turning.
cards.memory_hook: Signal, slow, no braking in turn

cards.front: What do you check before turning, and where must you finish?
cards.back: Before turning make sure it is safe by checking traffic to the front and rear and watching for pedestrians, and always finish the turn in the proper lane.

cards.front: What do you do when oncoming traffic will reach the intersection as you turn left?
cards.back: When turning left watch for approaching traffic in the opposite lane, and if that traffic will reach the intersection at about the same time as you, stop until it is safe to turn.

cards.front: Why keep the wheels straight while waiting to turn left?
cards.back: While waiting to turn left do not turn the wheels to the left, because a bump from behind could push your vehicle into oncoming traffic.

cards.front: When may you turn right or left on red?
cards.back: Where no sign prohibits a turn on red, traffic facing a red signal may turn right after a complete stop and yielding to pedestrians and traffic, and the same rule covers a left turn from a one-way street onto a one-way street.

cards.front: Where is it illegal to turn your vehicle around?
cards.back: It is against the law to turn your vehicle around near a curve, near the crest of a hill where a vehicle approaching within five hundred feet in either direction cannot see you, or where signs prohibit turning.

cards.front: When is turning around illegal near curves and hill crests?
cards.back: Turning around is illegal near a curve or hill crest whenever a vehicle approaching within five hundred feet in either direction cannot see you, and anywhere a sign prohibits it.

cards.front: How does a driver wait safely to turn left?
cards.back: A driver waiting to turn left keeps the wheels straight to avoid being pushed into oncoming traffic, and stops to let opposing traffic through when both would reach the intersection at about the same time.

cards.front: How do you angle park on your right?
cards.back: To angle park on your right, signal and slow down, stay parallel to the curb at least five feet out from the parked vehicles, steer sharply right when your front end is even with the rear of the space, pull slowly into the middle of the space, then straighten the wheel and roll forward until the front wheel barely touches the curb.

cards.front: How do you back out of an angle space safely?
cards.back: Backing out of an angle space is hazardous, so do not rely on the rear view mirror alone, move back cautiously watching for a pedestrian or vehicle that may suddenly appear if your view is blocked, and do not back across the center line.

cards.front: Which way do you turn the wheels when parking on a grade?
cards.back: When parking on a grade turn the front wheels toward the curb side of the highway so the vehicle will not roll, which means wheels to the curb when facing downhill, wheels away from the curb when facing uphill with a curb, and wheels to the right when facing uphill without a curb.

cards.front: How do you reinforce the parking brake on a grade?
cards.back: On a grade set the emergency or parking brake and reinforce it by placing an automatic transmission in park, or a manual transmission in reverse on a downgrade and in first gear on an upgrade.
cards.memory_hook: Brake and gear on a grade

cards.front: How close to the curb must a parallel-parked vehicle be?
cards.back: When parallel parking on a two-way street the right wheels must be parallel to and within eighteen inches of the right curb, when parking on the left side of a road the wheels must be within eighteen inches of the left curb, and the vehicle must face the direction of traffic and be centered in the space.

cards.front: How do you begin parallel parking?
cards.back: To parallel park, choose a space large enough, signal and stop even with the front vehicle about two feet out from it, then when traffic is clear turn the front wheels all the way to the right and back slowly toward the curb while looking behind you rather than relying on the mirror.

cards.front: How do you finish parallel parking, and how far from the curb?
cards.back: When your front bumper is opposite the rear bumper of the vehicle ahead, quickly turn the wheel all the way to the left and back slowly toward the vehicle behind without touching it, ending about six inches and never more than eighteen inches from the curb, then straighten the wheels, pull into final position and center the vehicle.

cards.front: What do you do when leaving a parallel parking space?
cards.back: When leaving a parallel parking space always signal to show your intentions and make sure traffic is clear before pulling back onto the roadway.

cards.front: Which way do the wheels turn facing downhill and uphill?
cards.back: Facing downhill the wheels turn toward the curb, facing uphill with a curb they turn away from the curb, and facing uphill without a curb they turn to the right.

cards.front: What distances frame parallel parking from start to finish?
cards.back: Parallel parking begins about two feet out from the front vehicle, ends ideally about six inches from the curb, and may never finish more than eighteen inches from it.
cards.memory_hook: Two feet out, six inches in

cards.front: How far out does angle parking start, and what is forbidden on exit?
cards.back: An angle-parking entry starts at least five feet out from the parked vehicles, while the exit must never back across the center line.

cards.front: Which gear holds a manual on a grade, and what about an automatic?
cards.back: On a grade a manual transmission is left in reverse when facing downhill but in first gear when facing uphill, while an automatic transmission simply goes into park.

cards.front: What is following distance, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Following too closely causes most rear-end collisions, the space ahead of your vehicle is the easiest space to control and is called the following distance, and you must weigh traffic speed and road condition to leave enough distance to stop when necessary.

cards.front: How do you apply the three-to-four second rule?
cards.back: To apply the three-to-four second rule choose a fixed object ahead such as a signpost, tree, overpass or bridge abutment, start counting one thousand one, one thousand two, one thousand three when the vehicle ahead passes it, and if you reach the object before finishing the count you are following too closely.

cards.front: What following distance applies in darkness, rain, ice or snow?
cards.back: When it is dark or raining the following distance should be at least four seconds, and when there is ice or snow stay at least six seconds behind the vehicle in front.

cards.front: How does following distance change with conditions?
cards.back: The following-distance count is three to four seconds in normal conditions, at least four seconds in darkness or rain, and at least six seconds on ice or snow.

cards.front: What should you check and do while backing?
cards.back: Before backing, check completely around the vehicle for people and obstacles, look to the front, sides and rear and keep looking to the rear while backing, do not depend on the mirror, and back slowly into the proper traffic lane.

cards.front: When is backing in a traffic lane acceptable, and what is never allowed?
cards.back: Backing up while in a traffic lane is not advisable except to back into a parallel parking space, and you must never back across other traffic lanes or through an intersection.

cards.front: How must a vehicle be parked relative to traffic, and what about double parking?
cards.back: A vehicle must always be parked in the same direction as traffic moves on that side of the street, completely off the traveled portion of the road, and double parking is illegal and discourteous.
cards.memory_hook: Park with traffic, no double parking

cards.front: What do you do when leaving a parked vehicle, and what danger does exiting bring?
cards.back: Whenever you park and leave the vehicle, turn off the engine, set the parking brake, lock the vehicle and take the keys, and because getting out on the street side is dangerous, look carefully for bicycles, motorcycles or larger vehicles that might hit your open door or you.

cards.front: What should you keep ready for meters, and how do you stay safe in a parked vehicle?
cards.back: Keep change easily accessible in the vehicle for metered parking, and if you must stay in the parked vehicle in a busy area keep the doors locked until you are ready to exit and stay alert to your surroundings.

cards.front: What backing is acceptable in a traffic lane, and what never is?
cards.back: Backing into a parallel space is the only backing the handbook calls acceptable within a traffic lane, and backing across other lanes or through an intersection is never allowed.

recap_hooks.text: Remember no parking: hydrant, driveway, crosswalk, no parking: crosswalk, stop sign, rail and no parking: excavation, bridge, mailbox
Remember improper turns cause crashes, prepare before the turn lane and signal, slow, no braking in turn
Remember angle parking entry, angle parking exit and wheels on a grade
Remember following distance basics, three-to-four second rule and four seconds rain, six snow
Remember look back while backing, backing in a traffic lane and park with traffic, no double parking
